title: Agent role manifest
description: The host-independent declaration of one worker role. This is the single source of truth for the role's model tier, reasoning strength, tool grant, and mutation class; every host agent file is generated from it by scripts/render_agents.py. Prose for the role lives in references/agents/<id>.md and is never duplicated here.

id.description: Agent name as hosts see it. Lowercase and hyphens only, because Claude Code and Cursor both derive the invocation name from it.

kind.description: What this manifest is FOR, which is not the same question as which position it fills. A worker is dispatched and returns a contract. The orchestrator dispatches workers, judges what they return, and talks to root through the mailbox. They differ in what `returns` and `mutation` even mean, so overloading `role` to cover both would make those fields conditional on a value buried elsewhere.

role.description: Which position this manifest fills. The three worker positions are a fixed three-agent loop, not an extensible registry: exactly one manifest each, and `kind` is what keeps that invariant enforceable now that a fourth agent exists which is not a fourth worker.

description.description: Host-facing trigger description. Must say what the role returns and that it is dispatched by root, so nothing invokes it as a general-purpose helper.

mutation.description: Portable capability class, and the thing hosts disagree about most. 'read-only' means no shell and no write tools. 'read-and-run' means a shell exists solely to rerun named acceptance commands. 'write-scoped' means edits are permitted, but only inside the brief's write paths — a boundary no host enforces, so a write-scoped role always carries an unenforced disclosure.

model.description: Cheapest-viable tier plus the ordered escalation path. Never 'inherit': every host defaults to inheriting the parent, which silently makes a cheap worker as expensive as root.

escalation.description: Ordered, strictly increasing tiers. Root advances exactly one step per recorded failure, never on a hunch.

reasoning.description: Reasoning strength. Expressed portably here; rendered into whatever each host actually supports, or disclosed as unenforced where it supports nothing.

tools.description: Portable tool intent. 'allow' is the complete grant; 'deny' is belt-and-braces for hosts that support a denylist, and documentation everywhere else.

allow.description: The full grant. An empty shell grant is expressed by omitting 'run-commands', not by granting it and asking the agent not to use it.

shell_purpose.description: Required by scripts/validate_roles.py whenever 'run-commands' is in 'allow'. Naming the single reason a shell exists is what stops it becoming a general grant.

must_not.description: Prohibitions the role carries. Entries that hooks/ can enforce mechanically are enforced; the rest are rendered into the agent's own instructions and into the enforcement disclosure.

returns.description: The contract this role must return, as a single fenced JSON block. Root validates the return with scripts/check_return.py before acting on it.

prose.description: Path to the canonical role prose. Host agent files point at it rather than restating it, so the role text exists in exactly one place.

modelTier.description: Vendor-neutral tier. hosts/<host>.json maps each tier to that host's own model id, so a role manifest never names a vendor model.

effort.description: Reasoning strength, in Claude Code's vocabulary because it is the most granular of the supported hosts. hosts/<host>.json maps these onto coarser scales, and declares when a host can express none of them.

toolIntent.description: Portable intent, not a host tool name. hosts/<host>.json maps each intent to concrete tool names; an intent a host cannot express is a rendering error, not a silent drop.
